title: De Morgan and short-circuits
summary: Negate conditions correctly with De Morgan, and let short-circuiting guard the checks that would crash. Delve learns where its map ends.

steps.title: De Morgan's laws
body: To negate a combined condition, flip each part **and** swap AND with OR:
In words: "not (tall and rich)" means "short **or** poor". "Not (raining or snowing)" means "not raining **and** not snowing".

These laws come from logic, not from any language, so they hold in C#, Python (`not (a and b)` == `not a or not b`) and JavaScript alike. You use them every time you turn "keep going while..." into "stop when...".

steps.prompt: Match each negation to its De Morgan equivalent.
steps.explain: Negating a comparison flips it: the opposite of `>` is `<=`, not `<`.

steps.prompt: A loop should keep running **while** the user has lives left **and** has not quit. Which is the condition for *stopping*?
steps.explain: Keep going is `lives > 0 && !quit`. Negate each part and swap `&&` for `||`: `lives <= 0 || quit`, and with lives never negative that is `lives == 0 || quit`.

steps.title: Short-circuiting
body: `&&` and `||` evaluate the left side first and **stop as soon as the answer is known**:
- `false && anything` is false, so the right side is skipped.
- `true || anything` is true, so the right side is skipped.
This is not just a speed trick. It lets the left side **guard** the right side:
Python      if count > 0 and total / count > 10:
When `count` is 0 the division never runs, so it cannot crash. Order matters: swap the two sides and the guard is useless.
Watch which calls actually happen below.

code: bool r1 = Check("A", false) && Check("B", true);
bool r2 = Check("C", true) || Check("D", true);
bool r3 = Check("E", true) && Check("F", false);

steps.prompt: Which checks run? What is printed?
code: bool r1 = Check("A", false) && Check("B", true);
bool r2 = Check("C", true) || Check("D", true);
bool r3 = Check("E", true) && Check("F", false);
steps.explain: A is false, so B is skipped. C is true, so D is skipped. E is true, so `&&` must look at F.

steps.prompt: `names` may be `null`. Which condition is safe?
steps.explain: The null check must come **first** with `&&`, so `.Length` only runs when `names` exists. With `||` a null `names` makes the left false and the right side runs and crashes.

steps.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `no average` without crashing.
steps.explain: The `count != 0` guard comes first, so the division is skipped when `count` is 0.

steps.title: Rewrite without the outer NOT
prompt: `Outside(x, lo, hi)` returns `true` when `x` is **not** in the range `lo` to `hi` (inclusive). It works, but reviewers asked for it without the `!( ... )` wrapper.
Use De Morgan to rewrite it with no `!` at all.
starter: bool Outside(int x, int lo, int hi)
solution: bool Outside(int x, int lo, int hi)
template: Dojo.Eq("Outside(1, 1, 10) is false (edges are inside)", false, Outside(1, 1, 10));
hints: Flip each comparison and swap `&&` for `||`.
The opposite of `x >= lo` is `x < lo`.

steps.title: Which check goes first?
steps.prompt: `map` is an array of rows and `x` may be `-1`. Which condition can never crash?
code: // A: map[y][x] == '#' || IsOutsideMap(x, y, width, height)
// B: IsOutsideMap(x, y, width, height) || map[y][x] == '#'
options: B: when the point is outside, `||` stops before it reads `map[y][x]`
A: the wall check is cheaper, so it should run first
steps.explain: `||` stops as soon as the left side is true. In B an outside point never reaches `map[y][x]`; in A the index runs first and throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` for `x = -1`.

steps.title: Where the map ends
prompt: Delve's map is a `string[]`: `map[y]` is row `y`, and `map[y][x]` is the character at column `x` in it (`'#'` is a wall). These two functions work on the inside of the map but have problems a reviewer flagged:

1. **`static bool IsOutsideMap(int x, int y, int width, int height)`** is written as `!( ... )`. Use De Morgan to rewrite it with **no `!` at all**. Inside means `0 <= x < width` and `0 <= y < height`.

2. **`static bool IsWall(string[] map, int x, int y)`** must treat every point **off the map** as a wall. Right now it crashes for `x = -1`. Make it one expression that calls `IsOutsideMap` (with `map[0].Length` as the width and `map.Length` as the height) and can never read outside the array.
starter: static bool IsOutsideMap(int x, int y, int width, int height)
return !(x >= 0 && x < width && y >= 0 && y < height);
static bool IsWall(string[] map, int x, int y)
return map[y][x] == '#' || IsOutsideMap(x, y, map[0].Length, map.Length);
solution: static bool IsOutsideMap(int x, int y, int width, int height)
return x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= width || y >= height;
static bool IsWall(string[] map, int x, int y)
return IsOutsideMap(x, y, map[0].Length, map.Length) || map[y][x] == '#';
template: Dojo.Eq("IsOutsideMap(0, 0, 5, 3): the corner is inside", false, IsOutsideMap(0, 0, 5, 3));
Dojo.Eq("IsOutsideMap(4, 2, 5, 3): the far corner is inside", false, IsOutsideMap(4, 2, 5, 3));
Dojo.Eq("IsOutsideMap(5, 1, 5, 3): width is one past the end", true, IsOutsideMap(5, 1, 5, 3));
Dojo.Eq("IsWall at (1, 1) is floor", false, IsWall(dojoMap, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("IsWall at (3, 1) is a wall", true, IsWall(dojoMap, 3, 1));
Dojo.Eq("IsWall at (-1, 1): off the map counts as a wall", true, IsWall(dojoMap, -1, 1));

forbid.message: No ! anywhere: De Morgan gets rid of it
One boolean expression per function: no if, no ?
Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)

hints: De Morgan: `!(a && b)` is `!a || !b`. And `!(x >= 0)` is simply `x < 0`.
For IsWall, put the check that protects the index on the left of `||`.

build.title: The edges of the map
build.unlocks: Walking off the edge of Delve now bumps into a wall instead of crashing.
